title: Non-Desarguesian Planes: The Moulton Plane Counterexample
description: Formalizes the Moulton plane (1902) — a non-Desarguesian affine plane over ℝ — and provides an explicit rational-coordinate counterexample showing that Desargues's theorem fails. Two triangles are in perspective from a point yet their corresponding-side intersections are not Moulton-collinear.

overview.historicalContext:
Girard Desargues (1591–1661), a Lyonnais architect and engineer in the orbit of Marin Mersenne, proved his perspective-triangle theorem c. 1639 in his now-rare *Brouillon project d'une atteinte aux événements des rencontres du cône avec un plan* (a small print run, of which most copies were lost; the work was reconstructed in the 19th century from a single surviving copy and from Philippe de la Hire's 1679 paraphrase). The theorem was first published as a stand-alone result by Abraham Bosse in *Manière universelle de M. Desargues pour pratiquer la perspective* (1648) and was rediscovered in the 19th century by Jean-Victor Poncelet (*Traité des propriétés projectives des figures*, 1822). In its modern form Desargues's theorem asserts: if triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are *perspective from a point* — that is, the lines $AA'$, $BB'$, $CC'$ all meet at a common point $O$ — then the three intersection points $P = AB \cap A'B'$, $Q = BC \cap B'C'$, $R = CA \cap C'A'$ are *collinear*. The theorem is self-dual, an instance of the duality principle that converts every projective theorem about points and lines into one about lines and points (formalized in this gallery's `desargues-theorem-oq-04`).

For over two centuries, Desargues's theorem was treated as a deductive consequence of the plane projective axioms (incidence, line-uniqueness, point-uniqueness). The shift came with David Hilbert's *Grundlagen der Geometrie* (1899) — the foundational text that made axiomatic independence a central question of geometry. Hilbert systematically asked, for each classical theorem, *which* axioms it depends on, and in §§22–30 of *Grundlagen* he proved that Desargues's theorem is necessary for the introduction of coordinates from a skew field (division ring) into a projective plane: any 'Desarguesian' projective plane (one in which the theorem holds) can be coordinatized by a unique-up-to-isomorphism skew field, and conversely. This left open the question whether every projective plane *was* Desarguesian — i.e., whether the theorem followed from incidence axioms alone.
overview.problemStatement: Can we formalize non-Desarguesian projective planes in Lean to show when Desargues's theorem fails? Desargues's theorem asserts: if triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are in perspective from a point (i.e., lines $OAA'$, $OBB'$, $OCC'$ are concurrent at $O$), then the corresponding-side intersections $P = AB \cap A'B'$, $Q = BC \cap B'C'$, $R = CA \cap C'A'$ are collinear. The Moulton plane (1902) satisfies all affine plane axioms but violates Desargues: `desargues_fails : ¬ MoultonCollinear P_pt Q_pt R_pt`.
overview.proofStrategy:
The formalization realises Moulton's 1902 4-page proof in six structural stages, each implementing one of the conceptual ingredients of the original argument as a self-contained Lean module.

**Stage 1 — Define the bent-line predicate.** `onMoultonLine m b P` is built as a two-level `Classical` if-then-else: ordinary line $y = mx + b$ when $m \leq 0$, bent line (slope $m$ on $x \leq 0$, slope $m/2$ on $x > 0$) when $m > 0$. `MoultonCollinear P Q R` is *disjunctive*: either all three points share an $x$-coordinate (vertical line) or there exist $(m, b)$ with all three on the same Moulton line. The disjunctive shape is forced by the slope-intercept formalism (vertical lines have undefined slope), and it directly drives the three-case structure of the main non-collinearity proof downstream.
keyInsights: **The bending rule is the minimal perturbation that breaks Desargues while preserving all affine plane axioms.** Moulton's 1902 insight was that the line geometry of $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be modified by a single piecewise rule — slope $m$ on $x \leq 0$, slope $m/2$ on $x > 0$, only for positive-slope lines — to break Desargues without disturbing any of the three classical affine axioms.

**$P$ and $R$ live in the ordinary regime; only $Q$ exercises the bend.** Sides $AB$ (slope $-2/5$), $A'B'$ (slope $-3/13$), $CA$ (slope $-2$), and $C'A'$ (slope $-5/2$) all have *negative* slope, so they are unmodified Euclidean lines in the Moulton plane and the intersection points $P = AB \cap A'B' = (-17, 9)$ and $R = CA \cap C'A' = (-6, 11)$ are computed by ordinary slope-intercept linear algebra.

**The contradiction reduces to an over-determined $2 \times 2$ linear system in $(m, b)$.** Assuming Moulton-collinearity of $P = (-17, 9)$, $Q = (27, 17)$, $R = (-6, 11)$ on a positive-slope bent line with left-slope $m$ and intercept $b$ produces three equations: $9 = -17m + b$ from $P$ at $x < 0$ (left-half slope), $17 = \tfrac{m}{2} \cdot 27 + b$ from $Q$ at $x > 0$ (right-half *halved* slope), and $11 = -6m + b$ from $R$ at $x < 0$ (left-half slope).

**$P, Q, R$ are Euclidean-collinear, confirming that classical Desargues holds in $\mathbb{R}^2$ — the failure is created by the bend alone.** A direct computation in the Euclidean plane shows that the slope from $P = (-17, 9)$ to $Q = (27, 17)$ is $\tfrac{17 - 9}{27 - (-17)} = \tfrac{8}{44} = \tfrac{2}{11}$ and the slope from $P$ to $R = (-6, 11)$ is $\tfrac{11 - 9}{-6 - (-17)} = \tfrac{2}{11}$ — the same slope.

Characterisation: Desargues's theorem holds in a projective plane iff the plane is coordinatizable by a skew field (division ring) — the Moulton plane's bent coordinatization is not associative, blocking this coordinatization

**Hessenberg's theorem (1905): Pappus implies Desargues.** Pappus's hexagon theorem — for points $A_1, A_2, A_3$ on one line and $B_1, B_2, B_3$ on another, the three intersections $A_1B_2 \cap A_2B_1$, $A_1B_3 \cap A_3B_1$, $A_2B_3 \cap A_3B_2$ are collinear — is *strictly stronger* than Desargues. Hessenberg's 1905 proof (*Math. Ann.* 61) shows that Pappus + incidence axioms $\Rightarrow$ Desargues, so every Pappian plane is Desarguesian.

**The dimension-2 vs dimension-$\geq 3$ dichotomy (Veblen-Young, 1908–1910).** Desargues's theorem is *automatic* in projective spaces of dimension $\geq 3$: Veblen and Young proved that in any projective space satisfying the basic incidence axioms with at least three independent points off any plane, Desargues's theorem holds for free.
**Coordinatization by ternary rings and the Hall plane (1943).** Marshall Hall, Jr. (*Trans. AMS*, vol.

**Why the bend is exactly halved: the unique minimal perturbation.** The Moulton line definition uses slope $m$ for $x \leq 0$ and slope $m/2$ for $x > 0$ when $m > 0$ — but why the factor $1/2$ specifically?
prerequisites: Affine and projective plane axioms: two-points-determine-a-line, two-non-parallel-lines-meet-in-a-point, parallel postulate (in the affine case), and the distinction between affine and projective completions (line at infinity)

Desargues's theorem: triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are *perspective from a point* $O$ (i.e., lines $OAA'$, $OBB'$, $OCC'$ concurrent) iff they are *perspective from a line* (the three intersections $P = AB \cap A'B'$, $Q = BC \cap B'C'$, $R = CA \cap C'A'$ are collinear) — see `desargues-theorem` for the standard $\mathbb{R}^3$ homogeneous-coordinate proof

Coordinatization theory: the Hilbert-Hall correspondence between geometric axioms and algebraic structures on the coordinatizing ring — Pappian $\Leftrightarrow$ commutative field, Desarguesian $\Leftrightarrow$ skew field (division ring), Moufang $\Leftrightarrow$ alternative algebra, general projective plane $\Leftrightarrow$ planar ternary ring (Hall 1943)

Hessenberg's theorem (1905): Pappus $\Rightarrow$ Desargues, giving the strict hierarchy Pappian $\subsetneq$ Desarguesian $\subsetneq$ all planes (the converse failing via non-commutative division rings like the real quaternions $\mathbb{H}$)

Wedderburn's little theorem (1905): every finite division ring is commutative, equivalently every finite Desarguesian projective plane is Pappian — so finite non-Desarguesian planes (Hall plane of order 9, Hughes planes, André planes) are the only finite witnesses for the strict containment Pappian $\subsetneq$ Desarguesian

Lean 4 piecewise-definition idioms: `Classical.propDecidable` to enable `if-then-else` on `Prop` (needed for the Moulton-line slope-sign case split), `by_cases h : m ≤ 0` for tactic-mode case analysis, and the `norm_num` / `linarith` / `linear_combination` arithmetic tactics that close every numeric goal in the 297-line formalization

Rational-coordinate linear algebra in $\mathbb{Q}^2$: explicit computation of line intersections via the slope-intercept formulas $y = mx + b$ and $y = m'x + b'$, the cross-product collinearity test $\det\!\begin{pmatrix} x_2 - x_1 & y_2 - y_1 \\ x_3 - x_1 & y_3 - y_1 …

mainTheorems.name: MoultonCollinear
mainTheorems.description: Three-point Moulton collinearity: either all three points share an x-coordinate (vertical line) or they all lie on some non-vertical Moulton line specified by left-slope m and intercept b.

mainTheorems.name: collinear_OAA'
mainTheorems.description: First perspectivity-from-O fact. Line OA has slope -3/2 ≤ 0, so it is an ordinary Moulton line (the bending only affects positive slopes).

mainTheorems.name: collinear_OBB'
mainTheorems.description: Second perspectivity-from-O fact, and the one where Moulton bending becomes operationally visible inside the perspectivity hypothesis: line OB has left-slope 2/3 > 0.

mainTheorems.name: collinear_OCC'
mainTheorems.description: Third perspectivity-from-O fact, dispatched by the vertical-line branch of MoultonCollinear: O, C, C' all have x = 0.

mainTheorems.name: PQR_x_distinct
mainTheorems.description: Excludes the vertical case from desargues_fails. The three intersection points P=(-17,9), Q=(27,17), R=(-6,11) have pairwise distinct x-coordinates (-17 ≠ 27 ≠ -6 ≠ -17), so no vertical Moulton line can contain all three.

conclusion.summary: The Moulton plane provides a fully formalized, axiom-free counterexample to Desargues's theorem in an affine plane over ℝ. The explicit rational-coordinate construction (Moulton, 1902) proves that Desargues is NOT derivable from the affine plane axioms alone — it requires that the coordinatizing structure be a field or division ring. The formalization uses only Mathlib real arithmetic (norm_num, linarith, linear_combination) — no topology, continuity, or algebraic geometry.
conclusion.implications: **Structural classification of projective planes.** The failure of Desargues's theorem characterises non-Desarguesian planes — those not coordinatizable by a skew field. Combined with the Hilbert-Hall coordinatization correspondence, the Moulton counterexample places projective planes into a strict hierarchy: **Pappian** (coordinatizable by a commutative field) $\subsetneq$ **Desarguesian** (coordinatizable by a skew field, possibly non-commutative) $\subsetneq$ **Moufang** (coordinatizable by an alternative algebra — adding the Cayley plane $\mathbb{O}\mathbb{P}^2$ as the unique non-Desarguesian Moufang plane) $\subsetneq$ **all projective planes** (coordinatizable only by a planar ternary ring). The Moulton plane is the historical and conceptual prototype of the bottom tier, and the gallery's `desargues-theorem-oq-01` (Desargues over commutative rings) and this entry (Moulton failure) together bracket the boundary between the top three tiers and the bottom one.
openQuestions: Can the Moulton plane be extended to a full *projective* plane by adjoining a line at infinity, and Desargues's failure transferred to the projective completion?
Can the smallest finite non-Desarguesian projective plane — the **Hall plane of order 9** (Marshall Hall, Jr., 1943) — be formalized in Lean as a sibling to this Moulton entry?

Can the *converse* coordinatization theorem be formalized: a projective plane satisfies Desargues's theorem if and only if it is coordinatisable by a *skew field* (division ring)? This is Hilbert's 1899 theorem (*Grundlagen* §§22-30), refined by Hall (1943) and Veblen-Young (1910).

Can the 1-parameter family of bent-line affine planes $\mathrm{Moulton}_\lambda$ — defined by the piecewise rule slope $m$ for $x \leq 0$ and slope $\lambda m$ for $x > 0$ when $m > 0$, with $\lambda \in (0,1)$ — be classified up to isomorphism, and the moduli space $\{ \lambda \in (0,1) \} / \sim$ formalized in Lean?
